topic: JVM Internals (Memory Model, G1/ZGC, Class Loading)

questions.question: What is the primary cause of this memory leak?
options: A) The `@Transactional` proxy retains a hard reference to the `REQUEST_BUFFER` field across transaction boundaries.
B) Web container worker threads (e.g., Tomcat execution pool) are pooled and reused, causing `ThreadLocal` values to persist indefinitely unless explicitly cleaned up via `ThreadLocal.remove()`.
C) The `static` modifier on `REQUEST_BUFFER` moves the byte array allocation directly into Metaspace, preventing Garbage Collection.
D) G1GC ignores `ThreadLocal` references during Young Generation collections, causing premature promotion to Old Generation.
questions.correct_answer_text: B) Web container worker threads (e.g., Tomcat execution pool) are pooled and reused, causing `ThreadLocal` values to persist indefinitely unless explicitly cleaned up via `ThreadLocal.remove()`.
questions.explanation: In web applications, web servers like Tomcat maintain thread pools (`http-nio-*`). When a request finishes, the worker thread goes back to the pool rather than dying. If a `ThreadLocal` variable is set without invoking `REQUEST_BUFFER.remove()` in a `finally` block, the reference remains bound to that worker thread's `ThreadLocalMap`. Over time, as all pooled threads execute this code path, large amounts of heap space become pinned and un-collectable.

questions.scenario: You are debugging a production issue where a payment processing service on Java 17 using the G1 Garbage Collector (`G1GC`) experiences intermittent latency spikes. The JVM configuration is `-Xms32g -Xmx32g`. GC logs reveal frequent Full GC cycles occurring even though total heap usage remains below 40%. The logs report frequent `To-space exhausted` messages along with continuous `G1 Humongous Allocation` occurrences for short-lived 9MB payloads.
questions.question: Why is `G1GC` triggering premature Full GC cycles, and what is the optimal fix?
options: A) Any allocation exceeding 50% of the G1 region size is categorized as Humongous and allocated directly into contiguous Old Generation regions, causing rapid heap fragmentation; increase `-XX:G1HeapRegionSize` to `16m` or `32m`.
B) The 9MB allocations fill the Thread-Local Allocation Buffer (TLAB); disable TLAB using `-XX:-UseTLAB` to force allocations into Survivor space.
C) The `To-space exhausted` error indicates Metaspace exhaustion; increase `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=1g` to resolve the issue.
D) G1GC concurrent marking threads are starving the application threads; switch to `ParallelGC` to guarantee throughput.
questions.correct_answer_text: A) Any allocation exceeding 50% of the G1 region size is categorized as Humongous and allocated directly into contiguous Old Generation regions, causing rapid heap fragmentation; increase `-XX:G1HeapRegionSize` to `16m` or `32m`.
questions.explanation: In `G1GC`, the default region size for a 32GB heap is 16MB. Any object that exceeds 50% of a region size (i.e. > 8MB) is treated as a 'Humongous Object' and bypasses the Eden space entirely, getting allocated directly into contiguous regions in the Old Generation. Frequent allocation of short-lived humongous objects causes rapid fragmentation of Old Gen regions and triggers concurrent marking cycles and costly Full GCs. Increasing `-XX:G1HeapRegionSize` to `32m` raises the humongous threshold to 16MB, allowing 9MB objects to be allocated in Eden/TLAB and swept efficiently by Young GC.

questions.scenario: You are debugging a production issue where a dynamic rule engine running on Spring Boot continuously generates and executes dynamic Java code using custom `ClassLoader` instances and CGLIB proxies. After a few days of operation, the application crashes with `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace`. Profiling confirms that millions of dynamically generated class metadata entries exist in Metaspace, but none of these generated classes are currently handling active requests.
questions.question: Which rule dictates why the JVM Garbage Collector has failed to unload these unused classes from Metaspace?
options: A) Metaspace memory is off-heap OS memory and cannot be reclaimed by JVM Garbage Collector cycles without a full JVM restart.
B) Dynamic CGLIB proxy classes are cached in the native JIT CodeCache, which holds strong roots to the underlying `Class` definitions.
C) A `Class` object can only be unloaded if its defining `ClassLoader`, the `Class` object itself, and all instances of the class are simultaneously unreachable by GC roots.
D) Spring dynamic proxies attach a strong reference to the JVM's System/App `ClassLoader`, preventing custom class loaders from being collected.
questions.correct_answer_text: C) A `Class` object can only be unloaded if its defining `ClassLoader`, the `Class` object itself, and all instances of the class are simultaneously unreachable by GC roots.
questions.explanation: Class unloading in the JVM has strict rules. A class stored in Metaspace can only be garbage-collected during a GC cycle if ALL three conditions are met simultaneously: 1) Zero instances of that class exist. 2) The `java.lang.Class` object is unreachable. 3) The `ClassLoader` that loaded the class is itself completely unreachable from any GC Root. If the application retains even a single reference to a custom `ClassLoader` instance (or a thread retains a context class loader reference), every single class loaded by that `ClassLoader` remains pinned in Metaspace indefinitely.
